analysis.one_liner: Requires complete withdrawal of all U.S. troops from Iraq within three months.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote or a hearing; it sat in two House committees until the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered every U.S. service member out of Iraq within three months of enactment, banned any money from being used to keep troops there as part of Operation Iraqi Freedom, and directed the Defense Department to bring home all private contractors and hand their work to the Iraqi government. It would have shifted security responsibility to a United Nations-led peacekeeping force funded partly by the U.S., barred any sale or privatization of Iraqi oil, banned U.S. covert operations against Iraq's government, and committed the U.S. to a reparations program for Iraqi deaths, injuries, and property damage. It was introduced by a single House member with two cosponsors and never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. service members and their families, who would have been brought home within three months instead of remaining deployed in a war zone; taxpayers, who would have stopped paying for occupation operations; and Iraqis, who would have gained a ban on oil privatization, an end to foreign contractor control of reconstruction work, and a funded reparations program. The bill's own findings cite a Congressional Budget Office estimate that withdrawal could cost as little as $10 billion.
analysis.who_benefits_short: U.S. troops, their families, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: All U.S. Armed Forces would have been completely withdrawn from Iraq and returned to the United States or redeployed outside the Middle East within three months of enactment.

The bill prohibited the use of any federal funds to deploy or continue to deploy troops to Iraq as part of Operation Iraqi Freedom, with exceptions only for the safe withdrawal, security consultations, and funding a U.N.-led peacekeeping mission.
It directed the Defense Department to simultaneously return all contractors and subcontractors and turn contracting work over to the Iraqi government, moving reconstruction jobs to local Iraqis.

It stated U.S. policy against privatizing Iraqi oil or other national assets and called for a reparations program for Iraqi deaths, injuries, and property damage, including aid for tens of thousands of Iraqi orphans.

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors and subcontractors operating in Iraq would have lost their contracts, which the bill directed be handed to the Iraqi government. Companies hoping to develop Iraqi oil fields would have been shut out by the ban on privatization. The U.S. would have borne the cost of the withdrawal itself and funding a U.N. peacekeeping mission, and opponents of rapid withdrawal would argue Iraqis could pay a price in security vacuums during the three-month pullout.

drawbacks.text: A complete withdrawal within three months would have left a security vacuum in Iraq with no guarantee that a U.N. peacekeeping force could form in time; the bill's own text acknowledges such a mission 'cannot take shape unless there is a peace to keep.'
The bill provided no residual U.S. force for counterterrorism or protection of U.S. personnel in Iraq, a gap critics of rapid withdrawal proposals raised throughout this period.

The bill directed spending on withdrawal and peacekeeping out of 'readily available existing funds,' which defense officials of the era argued constrained military readiness and could force cuts elsewhere in the budget.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to troops, their families, and taxpayers was direct and large: an end to deployments in an active war and a stop to occupation spending, with a CBO-cited withdrawal cost as low as $10 billion. The main cost was risk — a fast pullout depended on a U.N. peacekeeping force and an Iraqi political settlement that did not exist yet, and the bill had no fallback if neither materialized. The design was ambitious and detailed but rested on diplomatic steps Congress could not itself compel, which even sympathetic observers treated as a statement of principle more than an executable plan.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Armed Services and Foreign Affairs committees the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up, so it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on February 28, 2007, and it was referred to the House Armed Services Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Democrats.

The only activity after referral was a series of sponsor introductory remarks on the House floor between March 2007 and May 2007; neither committee held a markup or vote, and the bill never reached the House floor.
No further action was recorded for the remainder of the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors and subcontractors working in Iraq kept their contracts for the rest of the war, and the occupation and its spending continued for more than three more years after the bill died. The troops the bill would have brought home in three months remained deployed.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered a series of floor statements on it from March through May 2007.

for.name: 2 Democratic House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only support it drew in the House.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on February 28, 2007 and never reported it, held no markup, and never sent it to the floor.

against.name: House Foreign Affairs Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor, leaving withdrawal fights to appropriations bills instead.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote was ever taken; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, while most House Democrats supported shorter funding-based withdrawal timelines rather than this immediate full withdrawal.

industries.industry: Private military contractors and defense contractors in Iraq
industries.note: The bill would have ordered all U.S. contractors and subcontractors out of Iraq simultaneously with the troops and turned their contracts over to the Iraqi government. Their continued revenue from occupation work is money taxpayers pay and money that kept troops' support work in private hands.

industries.industry: Oil companies seeking access to Iraqi oil fields
industries.note: The bill declared U.S. policy against privatizing Iraqi oil or changing Iraqi law to enable it, closing off any post-occupation arrangement opening Iraqi reserves to foreign firms. Its findings called selling Iraqi oil assets during occupation a stumbling block to peace.

industries.industry: Defense industry dependent on Operation Iraqi Freedom spending
industries.note: A funding ban on deploying troops to Iraq would have cut off the occupation-driven demand for equipment, logistics, and services. The loss to contractors mirrors the saving to taxpayers.
